thinkers.name: Thales of Miletus
thinkers.summary: Thales of Miletus seems to have lived around the start of the 6th century BCE. Aristotle names him as the first person to look for the basic causes and principles of nature. He apparently wrote no book, so we know him mostly through later reports, and the famous story that he predicted an eclipse is almost certainly not true.
ideas: He held that water is the first principle (archē), the stuff from which everything comes.
He explained nature by nature itself, with no gods stepping in from outside.
He is reported to have said the magnetic lodestone has a soul because it moves iron, and that all things are full of gods.

thinkers.name: Pythagoras of Samos
thinkers.dates: fl. last quarter of the 6th c. BCE
thinkers.summary: Pythagoras grew up on the island of Samos and moved to Croton in southern Italy, where he gathered a community of followers. He wrote nothing, and later writers turned him into a near-divine figure, so his real views are hard to recover. In his own time he was famous for teachings about the soul and a strict way of life, not for mathematics.
ideas: The soul is immortal and is reborn again and again, possibly even in animals.
He founded a disciplined way of life with dietary rules, religious ritual and self-control.
The cosmos may be ordered by number and musical ratios, though how much of this was his own is doubtful.

thinkers.name: Heraclitus of Ephesus
thinkers.summary: Heraclitus of Ephesus was active around 500 BCE and is said to have written a single book, likely made up mostly of short, riddling sayings. He is best known for the ideas that things are always changing, that opposites belong together, and that fire is the world's basic stuff. He hints that he was self-taught, and he is hard to fit into any school.
ideas: Some things stay the same only by changing, like a river that remains a river because new water keeps flowing.
Opposites are bound together: sea water is healthy for fish but harmful for people.
One rational order, the logos, steers everything, and fire is its sign.

thinkers.name: Parmenides of Elea
thinkers.summary: Parmenides was born around 510 BCE in Elea, a Greek colony in southern Italy. He wrote a poem in which a goddess teaches a young man how to tell truth from mere belief. It has earned him a reputation as one of the deepest and hardest of the early Greek thinkers, and he is often seen as forcing later thinkers to answer his arguments.
ideas: There are only two routes of inquiry, that something is or that it is not, and you cannot know what is not.
Whatever truly is cannot come into being or pass away; it is whole, unshaken and complete.
Judge by reasoning, not by habit, eyes and ears; perception gives only belief, not knowledge.

thinkers.name: Democritus
thinkers.summary: Democritus was born about 460 BCE in Abdera in northern Greece. He built on a system begun by his teacher Leucippus: atomism, the theory that everything is built from tiny indivisible bodies moving in empty space. His works survive only in second-hand reports, and in antiquity he was known as the 'laughing philosopher' for prizing cheerfulness.
ideas: Only atoms and void are real; things differ by the shape, position and arrangement of their atoms.
Tastes, colours and heat exist by convention; the senses give a second-rate knowledge that reason must interpret.
The good is an inner state of cheerfulness, helped by moderating desire.

Ask me one question at a time and finish with a five-question quiz.

thinkers.name: Socrates
thinkers.summary: Socrates (469–399 BCE) wrote nothing, yet he changed how philosophy itself is understood. He spent his days in the Athenian marketplace, questioning anyone who would talk about courage, justice and the state of their soul, and he refused to take money for it. Athens executed him on a charge of irreverence toward the gods.
ideas: Knowing that you don't know is wiser than believing you know when you don't.
The health of your soul matters more than wealth, reputation or your body.
No one does wrong knowingly; wrongdoing comes from not knowing what is good.

thinkers.name: Xenophon
thinkers.summary: Xenophon was a soldier and historian who, like Plato, wrote works starring Socrates, including an Apology and the Memorabilia. He probably spent much less time with Socrates than Plato did, and he left Athens for good in 401. His Socrates is a practical adviser, and scholars still argue over how far that portrait can be trusted.
ideas: Socrates appears as a practical adviser, even on making money and running an estate.
Self-mastery (enkrateia, control over one's desires) is the foundation of virtue.
You are rich when you need little, not when you have much.

Ask me one question at a time and finish with a five-question quiz.

thinkers.name: Plato
thinkers.summary: Plato (429?–347 BCE) was a high-status Athenian and one of the most influential writers in the history of philosophy. He wrote dialogues, most with Socrates as the main speaker, so it is hard to say where his teacher ends and he begins. Philosophy as a rigorous, systematic study of ethics, politics, reality and knowledge can fairly be called his invention.
ideas: Behind the many things we see is a more real realm of Forms, perfect and unchanging patterns such as Beauty itself.
The soul is different from the body, and in some dialogues it recollects what it grasped of the Forms before birth.
Philosophy should improve political life: the Republic attacks rule by the many, while the later Laws gives non-philosophers real power as rulers.

thinkers.name: Aristotle
thinkers.summary: Aristotle (384–322 BCE) came from Stagira in northern Greece and studied at Plato's Academy until Plato died in 347. He later tutored the young Alexander the Great, then returned to Athens in 335 and founded his own school, the Lyceum, whose members became known as Peripatetics. About thirty-one of his works survive, ranging from logic and ethics to close observation of plants and animals.
ideas: To explain a thing fully, give its four causes: its matter, its form, what made it, and what it is for.
Nature has goals without a designer; living things develop parts for the sake of something.
Happiness is reason-guided activity done excellently, and humans flourish only within a political community.

thinkers.name: Theophrastus
thinkers.summary: Theophrastus (c. 371–287 BCE) was born on Lesbos, met Aristotle at Plato's Academy, and became his close colleague and his successor at the Lyceum. He is credited with over two hundred treatises, but less than a tenth survives. He worked to support, improve and extend Aristotle's system, often by setting out puzzles rather than final answers.
ideas: He wrote two large works on plants, the first systematic ordering of the plant world.
He questioned whether everything in nature has a purpose, pointing to things like insects that live only a day.
His Characters offers thirty short, often funny sketches of bad character types from everyday Athens.

thinkers.name: Alexander of Aphrodisias
thinkers.summary: Alexander of Aphrodisias was a Peripatetic philosopher active in the late second and early third century CE, and one of the heads of the philosophical schools in Athens. He wrote close commentaries on Aristotle that later commentators treated as a model. By reading Aristotle as one unified system, he helped shape the 'Aristotelianism' later attacked in early modern times.
ideas: Aristotle's philosophy is one unified whole, so apparent tensions should be smoothed over.
The human soul is the perishable form of the body, while the active intellect (the mind that is always thinking) is divine and separate.
Fate is simply the natural order of things, which leaves room for chance and for what is up to us, against Stoic determinism.
thinkers.prompt: Teach me Alexander of Aphrodisias as a short Socratic module. Start with the leading ancient commentator on Aristotle, active around 200 CE, then his three key ideas: Aristotle as one unified system; the soul as the body's form and a divine active intellect; fate as nature's order, against Stoic determinism. thinkers.name: Epicurus
thinkers.summary: Epicurus (341–270 BCE) was an Athenian citizen raised on Samos, who studied with a follower of Democritus. After teaching on Lesbos and at Lampsacus, he returned to Athens in 307/06 and bought the property known as the Garden, which gave his school its name. He built a complete system joining atomist physics to an ethics of calm pleasure.
ideas: The goal of life is happiness: freedom from bodily pain and from mental disturbance.
Death is nothing to us: while we exist death is absent, and when death comes we no longer exist.
Some desires are natural and necessary, some natural but unnecessary, and some empty, like fame or great wealth, which can never be satisfied.

thinkers.name: Philodemus
thinkers.summary: Philodemus of Gadara (ca. 110–ca. 30 BCE) studied at the Epicurean school in Athens and moved to Italy, probably in the 70s BCE. He was also a poet whose verse Cicero praised. Most of his philosophy comes from papyrus rolls found in the 18th century in a villa at Herculaneum, buried by the eruption of Vesuvius in 79 CE.
ideas: Anger comes in two kinds: a natural, mild pang and a destructive rage built on false beliefs.
Frank criticism is a skill: the leader of a community diagnoses friends' moral errors, like a doctor of the soul.
Music and poetry can give harmless enjoyment, but mastering their complex rules distracts from philosophy.

thinkers.name: Lucretius
thinkers.summary: Titus Lucretius Carus (mid-90s to mid-50s BCE) wrote On the Nature of Things (De rerum natura), a six-book Latin poem on Epicurean physics. Almost nothing is known of his life. His poem is our fullest source for Epicurean atomism and our only Epicurean source for the atomic 'swerve'.
ideas: Poetry is like honey on the rim of a cup: it sweetens a teaching that only seems bitter.
The soul dies with the body, so death is nothing to fear; we feel no dread about the time before we were born.
Atoms sometimes swerve by a tiny amount, at no fixed time or place, which lets them collide and form things.

thinkers.name: Zeno of Citium
thinkers.summary: Zeno of Citium founded the Stoic school around 300 BCE, named after the painted porch (stoa) in Athens where it met. He was a keen reader of Socratic dialogues, studied with the Cynic Crates, and was influenced by Plato's Academy. None of his works survives complete.
ideas: The goal of life is 'living in agreement': one consistent reason that is never at odds with itself.
Philosophy has three parts, physics, logic and ethics, that form one connected whole.
Some impressions grasp the truth so clearly that they cannot be false; he called this grasp 'cognition' (katalēpsis).

thinkers.name: Chrysippus of Soli
thinkers.dates: head of the school c. 230–206 BCE
thinkers.summary: Chrysippus of Soli (c. 280–207 BCE) was once a long-distance runner, studied under Cleanthes, and led the Stoic school from around 230 BCE. He is counted as the school's foremost theorist and systematizer. He is reported to have written over 150 works, but only fragments remain.
ideas: Everything is fated, yet assent is up to us: like a pushed cylinder that rolls because of its own shape.
The happy life and the virtuous life are one and the same.
He built a logic of whole statements (propositional logic) as an alternative to Aristotle's.

Start with the Stoa's great systematizer, who led the school from about 230 BCE, then his three key ideas: fate and assent, the cylinder analogy; the happy life is the virtuous life; a propositional logic beside Aristotle's. thinkers.name: Seneca
thinkers.summary: Seneca (c. 1 BCE – 65 CE) was born in Corduba in Spain and educated in Rome. His political life was dramatic: exiled to Corsica in 41, he later became Nero's tutor and then adviser. Writing in Latin letters, essays and consolations, he shaped how later generations understood Stoicism.
ideas: Philosophy is a practice of training and healing, aimed at the person making progress rather than the perfect sage.
Emotions like anger are judgments; 'moderate emotion' makes as little sense as moderate madness.
He writes within Stoicism but freely, following his teachers where they lead and borrowing from other schools when it helps.
thinkers.prompt: Teach me Seneca as a short Socratic module. Start with the Roman Stoic and adviser to Nero, c. 1 BCE – 65 CE, then his three key ideas: philosophy as therapy for someone making progress; anger as a judgment, and no 'moderate' emotions; an independent Stoic thinking in Latin. Ask me one question at a time and finish with a five-question quiz.

thinkers.name: Epictetus
thinkers.summary: Epictetus was born in the 50s CE in Hierapolis and spent part of his life as a slave in Rome. After gaining his freedom he taught philosophy, was expelled from Italy along with other philosophers, and set up his own school at Nicopolis in Greece, where he taught until his death around 135. His student Arrian wrote down his teaching as the Discourses.
ideas: Volition (prohairesis, our power to choose) is the true self, and nothing outside can force it.
Body, possessions and reputation are 'externals', neither good nor bad in themselves; what counts is how we use them.
Grief, fear and envy come from the false belief that happiness lies outside us; correct the judgment and the feeling changes.
thinkers.prompt: Teach me Epictetus as a short Socratic module. Start with a former slave who became a Stoic teacher at Nicopolis and died around 135 CE, then his three key ideas: volition as the free, true self; externals and how we use them; correcting judgments to change feelings. Ask me one question at a time and finish with a five-question quiz.

thinkers.name: Marcus Aurelius
thinkers.summary: Marcus Aurelius was born in 121 CE and ruled Rome as emperor from 161 until his death in 180, through wars, rebellions and plague. Part of his Meditations, notes written to and for himself, dates from his last military campaigns. Stoic teachers shaped him, and Epictetus is the Stoic author he singles out.
ideas: Only virtue is good and only vice bad; most of what we worry about is indifferent to our happiness.
Live as a citizen of the cosmic city, working for the good of all human beings.
Keep Stoic truths at hand in short sayings, like 'Erase impressions!', to stay free of pain and fear.

thinkers.name: Pyrrho
thinkers.summary: Pyrrho of Elis lived from around 365–360 to around 275–270 BCE and is said to have travelled with Alexander the Great to India. He wrote nothing; most of what we know comes through his follower Timon. Later Pyrrhonist skeptics took him as their inspiration, though he may not have been a skeptic in their sense.
ideas: To be happy, ask three things: what are things like by nature, how should we relate to them, and what follows?
Things are indifferent, unstable and undecidable (or at least we cannot tell them apart), so we should not trust our perceptions and beliefs.
Living without opinions leads first to speechlessness and then to tranquility.

thinkers.name: Arcesilaus
thinkers.summary: Arcesilaus became head of Plato's Academy and turned it skeptical, inspired by Socrates the examiner. Like Socrates, he wrote nothing. He was a sharp critic of the Stoics' theory of knowledge, and his attacks pushed Chrysippus to reshape Stoicism.
ideas: Examine someone's view using only their own premises, as Socrates did.
Any impression could be matched by a false one that looks the same, so there is no test of truth and we should suspend judgment about everything.
A skeptic can still act, guided by perception without adding belief, like walking through a door without judging 'here is the door'.

Start with the head of Plato's Academy in the 3rd century BCE who turned it skeptical, then his three key ideas: the Socratic dialectical method; no criterion of truth, so suspend judgment; acting without belief. thinkers.name: Carneades
thinkers.summary: Carneades was born in Cyrene in North Africa, studied in Athens at the Academy and with the Stoic Diogenes of Babylon, and became head of the Academy. In 156/5 BCE he went to Rome on an embassy, where he is said to have argued for justice one day and against it the next. He wrote nothing, but his ideas shaped the Academy until its end.
ideas: Act on the persuasive, and test important impressions harder, like poking a coiled rope in a dark room to check it isn't a snake.
Arguing for and against justice shows that its defenders lack the arguments they think they have.
He mapped every possible view about the goal of life, using the map to challenge the Stoics.

Start with the 2nd-century BCE head of the Academy, born in Cyrene, famous for arguing both sides, then his three key ideas: the persuasive, tested in stages; arguing both sides of justice; a map of all views on life's goal. Ask me one question at a time and finish with a five-question quiz.

thinkers.name: Sextus Empiricus
thinkers.summary: Sextus Empiricus was a Pyrrhonian skeptic who probably lived in the second or third century CE; his name comes from the Empirical school of medicine. Almost nothing is known of his life. His Outlines of Pyrrhonism is the fullest account of Pyrrhonian skepticism we have.
ideas: Skepticism is a skill: setting equally convincing arguments against each other until judgment is suspended.
Tranquility comes after suspending judgment, not by aiming straight at it.
Skeptics keep investigating, unlike dogmatists who claim to have found the truth and Academics who say it cannot be found.

thinkers.name: Plotinus
thinkers.summary: Plotinus was born in Egypt, studied with Ammonius Saccas in Alexandria and taught in Rome from 244 until his death in 270. He is usually seen as the founder of Neoplatonism. His pupil Porphyry gathered his writings into the Enneads (six sets of nine treatises).
ideas: All reality comes from the One, or the Good, a first principle beyond being itself.
Reality unfolds in levels (the One, Intellect, Soul), and each level is drawn back toward the Good by love.
Evil comes from below, not above: it arises when souls turn their attention toward matter instead of the higher world.

thinkers.name: Porphyry
thinkers.summary: Porphyry was born in Tyre in Phoenicia, studied with Longinus in Athens and then with Plotinus in Rome, whose Platonism he adopted. He edited Plotinus' Enneads and wrote the Isagoge, a short introduction to logic. He also defended vegetarianism, partly as a matter of justice toward animals.
ideas: Plato and Aristotle agree on the essentials, even where they differ in detail.
His Isagoge sorted how we classify things (genus, species, difference, property, accident) and became the standard way into logic for centuries.
Philosophy, not ritual, is what saves the higher, thinking part of the soul.

thinkers.name: Iamblichus
thinkers.summary: Iamblichus was a Syrian Neoplatonist, probably a student of Porphyry, and is sometimes called the second founder of Neoplatonism. He shaped the later system of the Athenian school. He criticised Plotinus sharply, took a darker view of the human soul and championed salvation through ritual.
ideas: The human soul descends fully into the body and cannot rise on its own; it needs help from the gods.
Theurgy, meaning sacred ritual done together with the gods, is the soul's main path to salvation, ahead of pure reasoning.
Mathematics, studied in the Pythagorean way, is a purifying and uplifting spiritual exercise.

thinkers.name: Proclus
thinkers.summary: Proclus led the Platonic school in Athens for almost fifty years and was the most authoritative philosopher of late antiquity. He wrote commentaries on Plato, Aristotle and Euclid and systematic works across philosophy. He played a crucial role in passing Platonism on to the Middle Ages.
ideas: His Elements of Theology builds the whole system step by step from the One, as a chain of proved propositions.
The old Greek myths and religious revelations can be shown to agree with the philosophy of Pythagoras and Plato.
The gods know future events without fixing them, because how something is known depends on the knower, not the thing known.

thinkers.name: Origen
thinkers.summary: Origen was a Christian scholar from Alexandria who wrote commentaries on scripture and made heavy use of allegory. Though later considered a heretic, he laid the foundations of philosophical theology for the church. He was taught by an Ammonius whom most scholars identify with Plotinus' teacher.
ideas: Scripture has deeper meanings beneath the literal words, which allegorical reading brings out.
God is not a body but bodiless mind, even when scripture calls him fire or spirit.
Souls stay free in their choices; misusing that freedom causes their fall, and he expected most souls to be purified after death.

thinkers.name: Augustine of Hippo
thinkers.summary: Augustine was born in Roman North Africa, followed the Manichean religion for nine years, and was won over to Christianity partly through reading the Platonists. He was perhaps the greatest and most influential Christian philosopher of antiquity. His Confessions is a philosophy written from the first person.
ideas: Faith comes first, and reason then works to understand what faith accepts.
Evil is not a substance but a lack or corruption of good.
Since the fall, humans cannot will the good by their own effort; only God's grace frees the will.

Ask me one question at a time and finish with a five-question quiz.

thinkers.name: Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite
thinkers.summary: Pseudo-Dionysius was a Christian Neoplatonist who carried pagan Neoplatonism, especially Proclus, into a new Christian setting. He wrote under the name of Dionysius, a first-century convert of St Paul, which gave his works near-apostolic authority. Modern scholars think he most probably studied with Proclus.
ideas: Every name for God must finally be denied, and then the denials too must be left behind.
Names like over-good and over-being praise God as one while showing God's many sides.
Angels and the church are ordered in ranked hierarchies through which the vision of God is passed down.

ideaSources.section: 3.5 On the Celestial and Ecclesiastical Hierarchies

thinkers.prompt: Teach me Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite as a short Socratic module. Start with a Christian Neoplatonist of around 500 CE who wrote under the name of a convert of St Paul, then his three key ideas: denying every name for God; the over-names that praise God; hierarchies of angels and church. Ask me one question at a time and finish with a five-question quiz.

thinkers.name: Boethius
thinkers.summary: Boethius was a Roman aristocrat who translated Aristotle's logic into Latin and wrote commentaries and textbooks on it. Accused of treason, he was imprisoned and probably executed in 526, and in prison he wrote The Consolation of Philosophy. He became, with Augustine and Aristotle, a basic author for the Latin Middle Ages.
ideas: Riches, status, power and pleasure are fortune's goods of little worth; true goods like virtue cannot be taken away.
God lives in an eternal present and knows all times at once, so his foreknowledge does not force our choices.
Aristotle's logic, passed into Latin through his translations, became the foundation of medieval learning.

ideaSources.section: 5. The Consolation of Philosophy: The Argument of Books I–V.2

thinkers.prompt: Teach me Boethius as a short Socratic module. Start with a Roman statesman and scholar of the early 6th century who wrote The Consolation of Philosophy in prison, then his three key ideas: fortune's goods versus true goods; God's eternal present and our freedom; handing Aristotle's logic to the Latin world. Ask me one question at a time and finish with a five-question quiz.

thinkers.name: Anselm
thinkers.summary: Saint Anselm of Canterbury was the outstanding Christian philosopher and theologian of the eleventh century. He is best known for the ontological argument for God's existence in his Proslogion. He also wrote on God's nature and on human freedom, sin and redemption.
ideas: Faith seeking understanding: an active love of God that seeks to know God more deeply.
God is that than which nothing greater can be thought, and such a being must really exist.
Freedom is the power to keep a right will for its own sake, not the power to sin.

thinkers.prompt: Teach me Anselm as a short Socratic module. Start with the leading Christian philosopher of the 11th century, then his three key ideas: faith seeking understanding; God as that than which nothing greater can be thought; freedom as keeping a right will. Ask me one question at a time and finish with a five-question quiz.

thinkers.name: Peter Abelard
thinkers.summary: Peter Abelard was the leading philosopher and theologian of the twelfth century, a famous teacher, poet and musician. He is arguably the greatest logician of the Middle Ages and the first great nominalist (someone who denies that universals are real things). His affair with Héloïse and his clash with Bernard of Clairvaux over reason and religion made him famous.
ideas: Universals are not things in the world but words; only individual things exist.
Only the agent's intention decides whether an action is good or bad; deeds in themselves are morally neutral.
Apparently contradictory authoritative texts can be reconciled through careful analysis of their concepts.
thinkers.prompt: Teach me Peter Abelard as a short Socratic module. Start with the brilliant 12th-century Paris teacher and logician, then his three key ideas: universals are only words; intention decides moral worth; reconciling clashing authorities by analysis. Ask me one question at a time and finish with a five-question quiz.

thinkers.name: Thomas Aquinas
thinkers.summary: Thomas Aquinas was a Dominican friar from near Aquino in Italy who studied in Paris and Cologne. He was the greatest figure in philosophy and theology of thirteenth-century Europe and epitomises the method of the new universities. He took inspiration from Aristotle and built a new system from it.
ideas: Natural reason can prove that God exists, for example by showing there must be a first cause.
What reason truly demonstrates cannot contradict Christian teaching, though some truths are known only by revelation.
Natural law is the way rational beings take part in God's eternal law, and it grounds morality.
thinkers.prompt: Teach me Thomas Aquinas as a short Socratic module. Start with a 13th-century Dominican friar and the great system-builder of the medieval universities, then his three key ideas: proving God through a first cause; reason and faith cannot truly clash; natural law as the root of morality. Ask me one question at a time and finish with a five-question quiz.

thinkers.name: John Duns Scotus
thinkers.summary: John Duns Scotus was a Scottish Franciscan who taught at Oxford and Paris and was nicknamed the Subtle Doctor. He shaped debates on religious language, universals and human freedom. He absorbed Aristotle but thought Aristotle's God left no room for divine choice.
ideas: Some words, like being, apply to God and creatures in the same sense; the difference is one of degree, with God infinite.
Things share real common natures, and each individual is made itself by its thisness (haecceity).
True freedom means having real alternatives at the very moment of choice.

ideaSources.section: 2.3 Divine infinity and the doctrine of univocity

thinkers.prompt: Teach me John Duns Scotus as a short Socratic module. Start with a Scottish Franciscan of the late 13th century known as the Subtle Doctor, then his three key ideas: words like being mean the same for God and us; common natures and thisness; freedom as real options in the moment. Ask me one question at a time and finish with a five-question quiz.

thinkers.name: William of Ockham
thinkers.summary: William of Ockham was an English Franciscan who worked at Oxford and London and later fled a papal investigation to the court of Ludwig of Bavaria. He is best known for nominalism and for the principle called Ockham's Razor. He also wrote on logic, natural philosophy, knowledge, ethics and politics.
ideas: Ockham's Razor: don't believe in more kinds of things than reason, experience or scripture require.
There are no universal things; only universal concepts and words, applied to similar individual things.
The pope is not above correction, and a heretical pope may even be removed with help from secular rulers.
thinkers.prompt: Teach me William of Ockham as a short Socratic module. Start with an English Franciscan of the early 14th century famous for his Razor, then his three key ideas: Ockham's Razor; only concepts and words are universal; limits on the pope's power. Ask me one question at a time and finish with a five-question quiz.

thinkers.name: Francesco Petrarca (Petrarch)
thinkers.summary: Petrarch was one of the founding figures of the humanist movement. He set out what became the standard humanist critique of scholastic philosophy and turned philosophy back toward the classical tradition and ethics. He influenced later humanists such as Salutati, Bruni and Bracciolini.
ideas: Scholastic philosophy is useless if it does not help us live a good life.
It is foolish to cling to a single authority, since all authorities can be wrong.
Stoic ideas, drawn from Seneca and Cicero, can serve as therapy against emotional distress.
thinkers.prompt: Teach me Francesco Petrarca (Petrarch) as a short Socratic module. Start with a 14th-century founder of the humanist movement, then his three key ideas: philosophy must help us live well; no single authority deserves blind trust; Stoic remedies for distress. Ask me one question at a time and finish with a five-question quiz.

thinkers.name: Lorenzo Valla
thinkers.summary: Lorenzo Valla was one of the most important humanists of his time and the author of a famous handbook of Latin style. He used his command of classical languages to criticise ideas and institutions. He exposed the Donation of Constantine as a forgery and compared Jerome's Latin Bible with the Greek New Testament.
ideas: Careful study of language and history can expose forgeries, such as the document behind the papacy's claim to rule lands.
Philosophy should fit common sense and ordinary language, so he cut Aristotle's categories down to three: substance, quality and action.
Christian love and blessedness can be understood as a kind of pleasure, using Epicurean ideas against Stoic virtue.
thinkers.prompt: Teach me Lorenzo Valla as a short Socratic module. Start with a 15th-century Italian humanist and sharp-tongued critic, then his three key ideas: language as a tool to expose forgeries; philosophy in ordinary language; a Christian ethics of pleasure. Ask me one question at a time and finish with a five-question quiz.

thinkers.name: Marsilio Ficino
thinkers.summary: Marsilio Ficino was one of the most famous philosophers of the Italian Renaissance and its most important Platonist. He translated all of Plato's works into Latin, and also Plotinus, writing commentaries along the way. He blended philosophical, religious and literary traditions.
ideas: True wisdom was handed down through an ancient theology, a chain of inspired sages in which Plato was a key link.
The human soul is immortal and longs to return to its divine origin, like a pilgrim seeking home.
Love flows from God into all things and binds them together.
thinkers.prompt: Teach me Marsilio Ficino as a short Socratic module. Start with the 15th-century Florentine who translated Plato into Latin, then his three key ideas: the ancient theology of inspired sages; the immortal soul longing for home; love binding all things. Ask me one question at a time and finish with a five-question quiz.

thinkers.name: Giovanni Pico della Mirandola
thinkers.summary: Giovanni Pico was a prince fully committed to philosophy and strikingly original. In 1486 he published 900 Conclusions for a public debate in Rome, but the pope halted it and legal proceedings followed. He is famous today for a speech, later titled the Oration on the Dignity of Man, that he never delivered.
ideas: In his Oration, God tells Adam he alone can make himself what he wants; yet the goal Pico sets is to become angel-like and finally merge with God.
He built a Christian Kabbalah (a reading of Jewish mystical teaching), even claiming magic and Kabbalah proved Christ's divinity.
He used the study of texts and history to attack astrology's claim to ancient wisdom and reliable prediction.

ideaSources.section: 2.5 Being and the One and Astrology

thinkers.prompt: Teach me Giovanni Pico della Mirandola as a short Socratic module. Start with a 15th-century prince and philosopher known for his 900 Conclusions and his Oration, then his three key ideas: what the Oration really asks of us; Christian Kabbalah; his attack on astrology. Ask me one question at a time and finish with a five-question quiz.

thinkers.name: Desiderius Erasmus
thinkers.summary: Erasmus of Rotterdam was the most important Christian humanist, combining Christian faith with classical learning. He edited the Greek New Testament and wrote The Praise of Folly. He broke with Luther over free will and favoured peace and compromise in the Reformation debates.
ideas: Return to the sources: read scripture and the classics in their original languages.
The philosophy of Christ: learned piety and simple devotion matter more than scholastic speculation.
Against Luther, the human will is very weak but, with God's grace, can still choose the path of salvation.
thinkers.prompt: Teach me Desiderius Erasmus as a short Socratic module. Start with a Dutch Christian humanist of the early 16th century, then his three key ideas: back to the original sources; the philosophy of Christ; a weak but free will, helped by grace. Ask me one question at a time and finish with a five-question quiz.

thinkers.name: René Descartes
thinkers.summary: René Descartes was a first-rank mathematician, an important scientist and an original metaphysician. He developed algebraic geometry and pictured nature as matter obeying a few universal laws. His view of an immaterial mind linked to the brain gave rise to the modern mind–body problem.
ideas: Doubt everything that can be doubted, even the senses, to find what is truly certain.
Even while doubting, I cannot doubt that I exist as a thinking thing, and what I perceive very clearly and distinctly is true.
Mind (whose essence is thought) and body (whose essence is extension in space) are two distinct substances.

ideaSources.section: 3.2 The mark of truth and the circle

thinkers.prompt: Teach me René Descartes as a short Socratic module. Start with a 17th-century mathematician, scientist and philosopher, then his three key ideas: doubt as the road to certainty; the thinking self and clear and distinct perception; mind and body as distinct substances. Ask me one question at a time and finish with a five-question quiz.

promptSources.section: 3.2 The mark of truth and the circle

thinkers.name: Baruch Spinoza
thinkers.summary: Baruch Spinoza grew up in Amsterdam's Portuguese-Jewish community and was expelled from it in 1656. He is among the most radical philosophers of the early modern period. His naturalistic views on God and the human being ground an ethics of mastering the passions, a democratic politics and a critique of sectarian religion.
ideas: There is only one substance, God or Nature, and everything else exists in it.
Everything, including our will, is fully determined by causes; there is no free will in the usual sense.
We find freedom and happiness by understanding our passions and so reducing their hold on us.
thinkers.prompt: Teach me Baruch Spinoza as a short Socratic module. Start with a 17th-century Amsterdam-born Jewish philosopher expelled from his community, then his three key ideas: one substance, God or Nature; everything is determined; freedom through understanding the passions. Ask me one question at a time and finish with a five-question quiz.

thinkers.name: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz
thinkers.summary: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz is known as the last universal genius, working in metaphysics, logic, mathematics, physics, law and history. He held that the only truly real things are simple, mind-like substances he called monads. He answered the mind–body problem with a harmony set up in advance by God.
ideas: Nothing happens without a sufficient reason why it is so and not otherwise.
God always acts for the best, so this is the best of all possible worlds.
The mind is not a blank slate but like veined marble: innate ideas shape what it can know.
thinkers.prompt: Teach me Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz as a short Socratic module. Start with a polymath of the late 17th and early 18th century, then his three key ideas: the principle of sufficient reason; the best of all possible worlds; the mind as veined marble. Ask me one question at a time and finish with a five-question quiz.

sources.section: 5.1 Monads and the World of Phenomena

thinkers.name: John Locke
thinkers.summary: John Locke was a British philosopher, Oxford academic and medical researcher. His Essay Concerning Human Understanding (1689) is one of the first great defences of modern empiricism and maps the limits of what we can know. In politics he argued that sovereignty lies with the people and called for religious toleration.
ideas: There are no innate ideas or principles; there is no good evidence for them.
The mind begins as a blank slate, and all our basic ideas come from sensation and reflection.
Legitimate government rests on natural rights and the consent of the people, through a social contract.
thinkers.prompt: Teach me John Locke as a short Socratic module. Start with a 17th-century British philosopher and political thinker, then his three key ideas: no innate ideas; the mind as a blank slate filled by experience; government by consent. Ask me one question at a time and finish with a five-question quiz.

thinkers.name: George Berkeley
thinkers.summary: George Berkeley was an Irish-born philosopher and Bishop of Cloyne, and a sharp critic of Descartes, Malebranche and Locke. He is famous for idealism, the view that reality consists only of minds and their ideas. He also wrote on vision, mathematics, physics and religion, and influenced Hume and Kant.
ideas: Ordinary objects are collections of ideas, and it makes no sense for them to exist unperceived.
We cannot form abstract general ideas by stripping away particular features, as Locke suggested.
Since our sensory ideas are not caused by matter or by ourselves, they must come from another spirit: God.
thinkers.prompt: Teach me George Berkeley as a short Socratic module. Start with an Irish philosopher and Anglican bishop of the early 18th century, then his three key ideas: to exist is to be perceived; no abstract general ideas; God as the cause of our perceptions. Ask me one question at a time and finish with a five-question quiz.

thinkers.name: David Hume
thinkers.summary: David Hume was a leading figure of the Scottish Enlightenment who applied the experimental method of the sciences to philosophy. He is famous for his skepticism, his naturalism and his challenges to religion. In his own time he was better known for his histories and essays.
ideas: All simple ideas are fainter copies of earlier impressions (vivid perceptions and feelings).
Reason cannot justify our expectation that the future will be like the past; custom or habit drives it.
Moral judgments come from feeling: we call a trait virtuous because viewing it gives us a particular pleasure.
thinkers.prompt: Teach me David Hume as a short Socratic module. Start with an 18th-century Scottish philosopher and historian, then his three key ideas: ideas as copies of impressions; induction rests on habit, not reason; morality grounded in feeling. Ask me one question at a time and finish with a five-question quiz.

thinkers.name: Voltaire
thinkers.summary: Voltaire was the pen name of François-Marie d'Arouet, a French writer and public activist who did much to define the Enlightenment. He wrote plays, stories and poems as well as philosophy, and championed Newton's science against the grand systems of Descartes and Leibniz. From the 1750s he campaigned publicly against what he called fanaticism and superstition.
ideas: No authority, however sacred, should be shielded from questioning by critical reason.
Science should describe and measure what we can observe, and leave out speculation about what cannot be seen (metaphysics).
Free speech and thought are worth defending, though the famous 'defend to the death your right to say it' line is not actually his.
thinkers.prompt: Teach me Voltaire as a short Socratic module. Start with the French writer and activist (1694–1778) who helped define the Enlightenment, then his three key ideas: no authority is above critical questioning; science should stick to what can be observed and measured; freedom of speech and thought deserves defending. Ask me one question at a time and finish with a five-question quiz.

thinkers.name: Jean-Jacques Rousseau
thinkers.summary: Jean-Jacques Rousseau was born in Geneva in 1712 and wrote on politics, education and human psychology, as well as composing music and writing novels. His central worry was how people can stay free when they depend more and more on each other, and on each other's opinion. He was often a dissenting voice within the Enlightenment, and his stress on feeling made him a forerunner of Romanticism.
ideas: People are good by nature but are corrupted by society, though what that natural goodness means is hard to pin down.
A legitimate state is guided by the general will: laws that come from all citizens and apply equally to all.
Education should follow the child's natural growth and let the child discover things, rather than impose lessons by authority.

ideaSources.section: 3.1 The idea of the general will

thinkers.prompt: Teach me Jean-Jacques Rousseau as a short Socratic module. Start with the Geneva-born writer on politics and education (born 1712) who questioned his own age, then his three key ideas: people are naturally good but corrupted by society; a legitimate state follows the general will, laws from all and for all; education should follow the child's natural development. Ask me one question at a time and finish with a five-question quiz.

thinkers.name: Denis Diderot
thinkers.summary: Denis Diderot was, with Voltaire, a leader of the French philosophes after 1750, and with d'Alembert he edited the Encyclopédie, meant to change the common way of thinking. In 1749 his writings got him jailed for three months in Vincennes prison. He did philosophy through plays, novels and art criticism as well as essays, and SEP calls him arguably the most sophisticated of the philosophes.
ideas: Knowledge should be gathered and shared as a living tool for changing minds, not as a dusty record.
We learn about nature through experiment and observation, not by abstract reasoning alone.
There is only one kind of stuff, matter, always in flux; living beings are temporary clusters of it (materialism).

ideaSources.section: 1.2 Ascendance as Writer and Philosophe through the Encyclopédie (1750–1765)

thinkers.prompt: Teach me Denis Diderot as a short Socratic module. Start with the French editor of the Encyclopédie (1713–1784), then his three key ideas: knowledge should be shared as a tool for changing minds; we learn about nature by experiment, not abstract reasoning alone; everything is changing matter (materialism). Ask me one question at a time and finish with a five-question quiz.

promptSources.section: 1.2 Ascendance as Writer and Philosophe through the Encyclopédie (1750–1765)

thinkers.name: Immanuel Kant
thinkers.summary: Immanuel Kant was born in 1724 in Königsberg, then capital of East Prussia, and SEP calls him the central figure in modern philosophy. His Critique of Pure Reason (1781) came near the end of the Enlightenment and tested what reason itself can and cannot know. The core idea running through his work is human autonomy, which literally means giving the law to yourself.
ideas: We know the world only as it appears to us, shaped by our mind's own forms such as space and time, never as things are in themselves.
Morality comes from reason: act only on a rule you could will as a law for everyone (the categorical imperative, a duty that binds whatever you happen to want).
Enlightenment means thinking for yourself rather than letting others think for you.
thinkers.prompt: Teach me Immanuel Kant as a short Socratic module. Start with the philosopher from Königsberg (1724–1804) who tested the limits of reason at the Enlightenment's end, then his three key ideas: we know things only as they appear to us, never as they are in themselves; act only on rules you could will for everyone (the categorical imperative); enlightenment means thinking for yourself. Ask me one question at a time and finish with a five-question quiz.

thinkers.name: Johann Gottlieb Fichte
thinkers.summary: Johann Gottlieb Fichte came from a poor family of ribbon weavers in Saxony, and reading Kant in 1790 changed his thinking. His first book appeared without his name and was hailed as Kant's own, which made him famous once the truth came out. At the University of Jena (1794–1799) he built a system he called the Wissenschaftslehre ('Doctrine of Scientific Knowledge'), grounded on the 'pure I' (the bare self).
ideas: Philosophy must start either from the free self or from things; Fichte started from freedom, since theory alone cannot settle the choice.
A thing that is not an object for our consciousness makes no sense, so even Kant's 'thing in itself' is posited by the mind.
You become a self only when another free person calls on you to respect their freedom, so mutual recognition is part of selfhood.

ideaSources.section: 3. The Starting Point of the Jena Wissenschaftslehre

thinkers.prompt: Teach me Johann Gottlieb Fichte as a short Socratic module. Start with the Jena philosopher (1762–1814) who rebuilt Kant's idealism on the free self, then his three key ideas: philosophy should start from the free self; there is no thing in itself beyond consciousness; we become selves through mutual recognition. Ask me one question at a time and finish with a five-question quiz.

promptSources.section: 3. The Starting Point of the Jena Wissenschaftslehre

thinkers.name: Friedrich Wilhelm Joseph von Schelling
thinkers.summary: Friedrich Wilhelm Joseph von Schelling was, with Fichte and Hegel, one of the three most influential German Idealists. He changed his views so often that he has been called a philosophical Proteus, yet SEP stresses that he was a rigorous thinker. He is remembered for his philosophy of nature, his view that the thinking self is never fully transparent to itself, and his later critique of Hegel.
ideas: Nature is not dead matter but a productive whole that includes us, and conscious mind grows out of it.
Subject and object, mind and world, must at root be one, or knowledge could never connect them (his 'identity philosophy').
Pure thought cannot capture real existence on its own, which is why he criticized Hegel's complete system.

ideaSources.section: 5. Positive and Negative Philosophy, and the Critique of Hegel

thinkers.prompt: Teach me Friedrich Wilhelm Joseph von Schelling as a short Socratic module. Start with the German Idealist (1775–1854) of nature, art and the critique of Hegel, then his three key ideas: nature is a living, productive whole from which mind emerges; mind and world are at root the same; pure thought cannot capture real existence, against Hegel. Ask me one question at a time and finish with a five-question quiz.

thinkers.name: G. W. F. Hegel
thinkers.summary: Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel, born in Stuttgart in 1770, studied alongside Hölderlin and Schelling and became the most systematic of the German Idealists. After the Phenomenology of Spirit (1807) he went on to celebrity in Berlin, where he died in 1831. He is best known for seeing history as purposeful development, an idea Marx later turned into a materialist theory.
ideas: Thought moves forward through contradiction: each way of seeing the world breaks down and gives rise to a fuller one.
I become aware of myself as a subject only through mutual recognition with other subjects.
Freedom is realized in shared social life ('ethical life'): family, civil society and the state, not only in private rights or conscience.
thinkers.prompt: Teach me G. W. F. Hegel as a short Socratic module. Start with the most systematic German Idealist (1770–1831), who read history as purposeful development, then his three key ideas: thought advances as each view breaks down on its own contradictions; self-consciousness depends on mutual recognition; freedom is realized in ethical life: family, civil society and state. Ask me one question at a time and finish with a five-question quiz.

thinkers.name: Jeremy Bentham
thinkers.summary: Jeremy Bentham was a jurist and political reformer, the philosopher most tied to the founding of modern utilitarianism. He gave the theory its secular, systematic form, especially in An Introduction to the Principles of Morals and Legislation (printed 1780, published 1789). He wrote on law, punishment, prisons, economics, education and democracy, aiming at a complete legal code based on utility.
ideas: Pleasure and pain govern us, and the right action is the one that tends to increase happiness.
A pleasure or pain can be weighed by its intensity, duration, certainty, nearness, fruitfulness, purity and how many people it reaches (the 'felicific calculus').
Laws should be judged only by the harm or good they do, so mere dislike of a practice is no reason to punish it.
thinkers.prompt: Teach me Jeremy Bentham as a short Socratic module. Start with the jurist and reformer (1748–1832) who founded systematic utilitarianism, then his three key ideas: pleasure and pain govern us, and right acts increase happiness; pleasures and pains can be weighed (the felicific calculus); laws should be judged by harm and good, not by dislike. Ask me one question at a time and finish with a five-question quiz.

thinkers.name: John Stuart Mill
thinkers.summary: John Stuart Mill was, according to SEP, the most influential English-language philosopher of the nineteenth century: a naturalist, a utilitarian and a liberal. His father, an ally of Bentham, gave him an intensely demanding education; at twenty Mill suffered a mental crisis and found relief in Romantic poetry. His major works include On Liberty (1859) and Utilitarianism (1861).
ideas: Some pleasures, such as those of the mind, are higher in quality than merely bodily ones.
The only good reason for society to interfere with someone's liberty is self-protection, and he defended this on utilitarian grounds.
Discrimination against women harms overall happiness; he likened the marriage law of his day to slavery.

thinkers.prompt: Teach me John Stuart Mill as a short Socratic module. Start with the London-born philosopher (1806–1873) who refined Bentham's utilitarianism and defended liberty, then his three key ideas: some pleasures are higher in quality than others; society may limit liberty only for self-protection; the subjection of women is wrong and harmful. Ask me one question at a time and finish with a five-question quiz.

thinkers.name: Henry Sidgwick
thinkers.summary: Henry Sidgwick spent his whole career at Cambridge, and in 1869 resigned his fellowship because he could no longer in conscience affirm the Church of England's articles. His The Methods of Ethics (1874) is seen as the culmination of classical utilitarianism, and some have called it the best treatise on moral theory ever written. He also worked on economics, politics, education and psychical research.
ideas: Everyday moral reasoning mixes three methods, egoism, intuited rules and utilitarianism, and he argued utilitarianism is the most basic.
From the point of view of the universe, no one's good matters more than anyone else's.
Reason seems to back both self-interest and the general good, and he could not fully reconcile them (the 'dualism of practical reason').
thinkers.prompt: Teach me Henry Sidgwick as a short Socratic module. Start with the Cambridge moral philosopher (1838–1900) whose Methods of Ethics capped classical utilitarianism, then his three key ideas: of ethics' three methods, utilitarianism is the most basic; no one's good matters more from the point of view of the universe; reason backs both self-interest and the general good. Ask me one question at a time and finish with a five-question quiz.

thinkers.name: Karl Marx
thinkers.summary: Karl Marx is often seen mainly as a revolutionary, but he was trained as a philosopher, with a doctorate in ancient philosophy, and engaged closely with Hegel. His work covers human nature and alienation, a theory of history, a critique of capitalism, ideology, the state and a predicted communist future. He refused to sketch communism in detail, holding that history itself would deliver it.
ideas: Under capitalism work is alienated: workers lose control of their products, their activity, each other and their own human nature.
A society's economic structure explains its politics, law and ideas, and when it holds back productive power it is overturned.
Religion is the 'opium of the people', a comforting illusion that will fade once material life is freed.
thinkers.prompt: Teach me Karl Marx as a short Socratic module. Start with the philosopher and revolutionary (1818–1883) who turned Hegel's history toward material life, then his three key ideas: work under capitalism is alienated; the economic structure shapes society and is overturned when it fetters production; religion is a comforting illusion rooted in material life. Ask me one question at a time and finish with a five-question quiz.

thinkers.name: Friedrich Engels
thinkers.summary: Friedrich Engels was Marx's lifelong collaborator, a leading figure in early socialist politics and a self-taught writer on history, science and philosophy. He wrote The Condition of the Working-Class in England (1845) and co-wrote The German Ideology and the Communist Manifesto (1848) with Marx. He called himself Marx's 'second fiddle', but SEP stresses his originality, and how far his views differ from Marx's is still debated.
ideas: Materialism means being comes before thinking and nature before mind, and he applied this well beyond economic history.
Nature itself is historical, always in process; he saw Darwin's work as a parallel to what Marx did for society.
Family and kinship belong to society's material base, alongside economic production.

thinkers.name: Søren Kierkegaard
thinkers.summary: Søren Kierkegaard was born in Copenhagen in 1813 and wrote mostly in the 1840s, across philosophy, theology, psychology and social critique. Anxiety is the dizziness of freedom: being drawn to and repelled by our own possibilities.

thinkers.name: Friedrich Nietzsche
thinkers.summary: Friedrich Nietzsche was a German philosopher and cultural critic who published mostly in the 1870s and 1880s. He is famous for fierce attacks on traditional European morality and religion, often by exposing the hidden psychology behind received ideas. He also proposed new values he hoped would renew culture, and SEP's existentialism entry counts him among the movement's nineteenth-century pioneers.

Imagine living your life over and over forever; on one influential reading, your reaction tests how much you value your life (eternal recurrence).

thinkers.name: Jean-Paul Sartre
thinkers.summary: Jean-Paul Sartre was, with Simone de Beauvoir, the most popular voice of mid-twentieth-century French existentialism, and a novelist, playwright and public intellectual. His treatise Being and Nothingness (1943) is called the defining work of the movement, and his 1945 lecture Existentialism is a Humanism drew huge crowds. ideas: Existence precedes essence: we turn up first and define ourselves afterward through our choices.
We are 'condemned' to be free: no fact about our situation fixes how we respond to it, so we are responsible.
Bad faith is self-deception: denying either our freedom or the facts of our situation.

thinkers.name: Simone de Beauvoir
thinkers.summary: Simone de Beauvoir was a philosopher, novelist, feminist and activist, and one of the major figures of post-war French existentialism. She is best known for The Second Sex (1949), a founding text of feminist philosophy. She called herself an author rather than a philosopher, but scholarship has secured her place as a thinker in her own right, not merely Sartre's helper.

I cannot live my freedom without affirming the freedom of others; evil lies in denying freedom.
Losing God does not mean anything goes: with no one to pardon us, we are fully responsible for what we do.

thinkers.name: Albert Camus
thinkers.summary: Albert Camus was a journalist, novelist, playwright and essayist who more than once denied being a philosopher. His Myth of Sisyphus sits squarely in the existentialist tradition, yet he denied being an existentialist and wrote against Kierkegaard, Jaspers and Heidegger. He won the Nobel Prize for literature in 1957 and died in a car accident in 1960.
ideas: The absurd is the clash between our need to ask what life means and a universe that gives no answer.
The answer to absurdity is neither suicide nor false hope but living fully aware and unbowed, like Sisyphus with his rock.
Revolt against injustice creates shared values and solidarity: 'I revolt, therefore we are'.

thinkers.name: Charles Sanders Peirce
thinkers.summary: Charles Sanders Peirce, born in Cambridge, Massachusetts, founded American pragmatism, later calling his version 'pragmaticism' to set it apart from James's and Dewey's. He earned his living for 32 years at the U.S. Coast and Geodetic Survey but saw logic and scientific philosophy as his true calling. He wrote on an enormous range of subjects, from mathematics and astronomy to psychology and economics.
ideas: To make an idea clear, consider the practical effects you would expect from its object; those effects are its whole meaning (the pragmatic maxim).
Truth is the opinion that everyone who investigates would ultimately agree on.
Science works by abduction (guessing a hypothesis that explains a surprise), then deduction of what should follow, then induction (testing).

thinkers.name: William James
thinkers.summary: William James worked across physiology, psychology and philosophy; his Principles of Psychology (1890) gave us the 'stream of thought'. A close friend of Peirce, he developed and popularized pragmatism, notably in his 1907 lectures Pragmatism. He also wrote on religion in The Varieties of Religious Experience (1902).
ideas: A dispute that makes no practical difference either way is idle; pragmatism is a method for settling such disputes.
True ideas are those that prove good to believe and help us get into satisfactory relation with the rest of our experience.
When a choice is forced and momentous and the evidence is not in, we may have a 'right to believe', since belief can help bring about what it believes.

thinkers.name: John Dewey
thinkers.summary: John Dewey was, with Peirce and James, one of pragmatism's founders and arguably the most prominent American intellectual of the first half of the twentieth century. He wrote on ethics, logic, metaphysics, art and religion, and his ideas on education and democracy had global reach. He preferred to call his view 'cultural naturalism', set within a Darwinian picture of living beings in their environments.
ideas: Inquiry starts from a felt problem and, through hypotheses and testing, turns an unsettled situation into a settled one.
Children learn best by actively working on real problems, not by passively receiving what others know.
Democracy is more than voting: it is a way of living together and sharing experience.

thinkers.name: Richard Rorty
thinkers.summary: Richard Rorty developed a distinctive and controversial pragmatism and helped spark its revival from the 1970s, often called neopragmatism. In Philosophy and the Mirror of Nature (1979) he attacked the idea of knowledge as the mind mirroring an outside world. He drew most on Dewey, though many pragmatist scholars dispute his readings and even his right to the label.
ideas: Knowledge is not the mind mirroring the world, and philosophy should drop that picture.
There is little of substance to say about truth; we test vocabularies by how well they help us reach our goals.
A liberal ironist knows her deepest descriptions are contingent, and holds that cruelty is the worst thing we do.

thinkers.name: Edmund Husserl
thinkers.summary: Husserl is described as the founding father of phenomenology. Trained first in mathematics, he turned to philosophy after hearing Franz Brentano, and saw his Logical Investigations (1900–01) as his breakthrough. Under the Nazi regime he was barred from teaching and publishing because of his Jewish ancestry.
ideas: Consciousness is always consciousness of something: experience is directed at objects through meanings.
To study experience, bracket the question of whether the world exists (the epoché) and describe how things are given.
Science grows out of the everyday lifeworld, and treating only the measurable as real alienates science from human experience.

thinkers.name: Martin Heidegger
thinkers.summary: Heidegger was Husserl's assistant and later his successor at Freiburg, and his Being and Time (1927) became one of the most influential books in 20th-century European philosophy. His driving question was the meaning of being. His support for the Nazi movement is well documented and still shapes how his work is read.

We are always already in the world, and things first show up as usable equipment, like a hammer, rather than as objects we stare at.

The lived body is not a mere physical thing; through it we are directed toward the world and our tasks in it.

He aimed to show that arithmetic rests on logic alone (logicism), though one axiom he added turned out to be inconsistent.

thinkers.summary: Beauvoir was a philosopher, novelist, feminist and activist, and a major figure in French existentialism after the war. She is best known for The Second Sex (1949). She was long treated as a helper to Sartre's ideas rather than a thinker in her own right, a view that decades of scholarship, mostly by feminist scholars, have overturned.
ideas: Woman has been made the Other, while man is treated as the essential being.
'One is not born but becomes a woman': a line many see as pointing to the sex-gender distinction.
Evil lies in denying freedom, our own and others', so we are responsible for each other's freedom.
